==English==
{{wp}}

===Etymology===
{{ety|en|:inh|enm:trade<ety:der<gml: trade<ety:der<osx:trada>>>>|tree=+}}
From {{inh|en|enm|trade|t=path, course of conduct}}, introduced into English by Hanseatic merchants, from {{der|en|gml|trade|t=track, course}}, from {{der|en|osx|trada|t=spoor, track}}, from {{der|en|gmw-pro|*tradu}}, from {{der|en|gem-pro|*tradō|t=track, way}}, and cognate with {{cog|ang|tredan|t=to tread}}; ultimately from {{der|en|ine-pro|*dreh₂-|t=to tread, walk, step, run}}. {{displaced|enm|chaffare}}.

Cognate with {{cog|nl|trade}}, {{m|nl|tra|t=path, trail, course, trade}}, {{cog|nds-de|Traad|t=track, wagon trail}}, {{cog|lb|Tratt|t=step, pace}}, {{cog|is|tröð|t=a lane between fences, enclosure, pen}}.

===Pronunciation===
* {{IPA|en|/tɹeɪd/|a=RP,GA}}
* {{audio|en|En-uk-trade.ogg|a=RP}}
* {{audio|en|LL-Q1860 (eng)-Naomi Persephone Amethyst (NaomiAmethyst)-trade.wav|a=GA}}
* {{audio|en|En-us-trade.ogg|a=GA}}
* {{rhymes|en|eɪd|s=1}}
* {{homophones|en|trayed}}

===Noun===
{{en-noun|~}}

# {{lb|en|uncountable}} The [[buying]] and [[selling]] of [[goods]] and [[services]] on a [[market]].
#: {{syn|en|commerce}}
# {{lb|en|countable}} A particular instance of [[buy]]ing or [[sell]]ing, or a series of related transactions executed as a single investment.
#: {{syn|en|deal|barter}}
#: {{ux|en|I did no '''trades''' with them once the rumors started.}}
# {{lb|en|countable}} An idea or strategy for an investment on a market.
#: {{ux|en|"Sell America" is the latest '''trade''' on Wall Street.}}
# {{lb|en|countable}} An instance of [[barter]]ing items in [[exchange]] for one another.
# {{lb|en|countable}} Those who [[perform]] a particular kind of [[skilled]] work.
#: {{syn|en|business}}
#: {{ux|en|The skilled '''trades''' were the first to organize modern labor unions.}}
# {{lb|en|countable}} Those engaged in an industry or group of related industries.
#: {{ux|en|It is not a retail showroom. It is only for the '''trade'''.}}
# {{senseid|en|skilled practice of a practical occupation}} {{lb|en|countable}} The skilled practice of a practical [[occupation]].
#: {{syn|en|craft}}
#: {{ux|en|He learned his '''trade''' as an [[apprentice]].}}
# {{lb|en|countable|or|uncountable}} An [[occupation]] in the [[secondary sector]], as opposed to an [[agricultural]], [[professional]] or [[military]] one.
#: {{ux|en|After failing his entrance exams, he decided to go into a '''trade'''.}}
#: {{ux|en|Most veterans went into '''trade''' when the war ended.}}
# {{lb|en|uncountable|UK}} The [[business]] given to a [[commercial]] [[establishment]] by its customers.
#: {{syn|en|business|takings|custom|footfall|patronage}}
#: {{ux|en|Even before noon there was considerable '''trade'''.}}
#: {{ux|en|'''Trade''' has been down in this cold weather.}}
#: {{ux|en|The gift shop relies on passing '''trade''' from tourists.}}
# {{lb|en|mostly|in the plural}} [[steady|Steady]] [[wind]]s blowing from east to west above and below the [[equator]].
#: {{ux|en|They rode the '''trades''' going west.}}
#* {{quote-book|en|year=1826|author=James Horsburgh|title=India Directory, Or Directions for Sailing to and from the East Indies, China, New Holland, Cape of Good Hope, Brazil and the Interjacent Ports|page=28|text=Calms and variable winds, are also experienced during every month of the year, in the space between the '''trades''';{{...}} the vicinity of the north-east '''trade''' seems most liable to them.|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ctJYAAAAcAAJ&pg=PA28|origyear=1816}}
# {{lb|en|only as plural}} A publication intended for participants in an industry or related group of industries.
#: {{ux|en|Rumors about layoffs are all over the '''trades'''.}}
# {{lb|en|uncountable|gay slang}} A [[masculine]] man available for [[casual sex]] with men, often for pay. {{non-gloss|(Compare ''[[rough trade]]''.)}}
#: {{ux|en|Not you tryna impress plumber '''trade'''.}}
#: {{ux|en|Josh picked up some '''trade''' last night.}}
# {{lb|en|obsolete|uncountable}} Instruments of any occupation.
# {{short for|en|trade paperback}}
# {{lb|en|mining}} Refuse or rubbish from a mine.
# {{lb|en|obsolete}} A track or trail; a way; a path; [[passage]].
#* {{quote-book|en|year=1557|author=w:Henry Howard, Earl of Surrey|title=The Second Book of Virgil's Æneid| passage=A postern with a blind wicket there was, / A common '''trade''' to pass through Priam's house}}
# {{lb|en|obsolete}} A course; a custom; a practice; an occupation.
#* {{quote-book|en|year=1655|author=w:Philip Massinger; {{w|John Fletcher (playwright)|John Fletcher}}|title=w:A Very Woman|passage=Long did I love this lady, / Long was my travel, long my '''trade''' to win her.}}
#* {{RQ:Shakespeare Measure|III|i|passage=Thy sin's not accidental but a '''trade'''.}}

===Verb===
{{en-verb}}

# {{lb|en|ambitransitive}} To [[engage]] in [[#Noun|trade]]. {{+obj|en|&transitive/:in<something> + :with<somebody>}}
#: {{syn|en|deal}}
#: {{ux|en|This company '''trades''' (in) precious metal.}}
#: {{ux|en|He withdrew money to his bank account after several years of '''trading''' stocks on E-Trade.}}
#* {{quote-book|en|year=1727|author=John Arbuthnot|title=Tables of Ancient Coins, Weights and Measures|page=248|text={{...}}a free port, where Nations warring with one another resorted with their Goods, and '''traded''' as in a neutral Country.|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=UmBMAAAAcAAJ&pg=PA248}}
# {{lb|en|finance|intransitive|copulative}} To be traded at a certain price or under certain conditions.
#: {{ux|en|Apple is '''trading''' at $200.}}
#: {{ux|en|ExxonMobil '''trades''' on the NYSE.}}
#: {{ux|en|The stock is '''trading''' rich relative to its sector.}}
# {{lb|en|transitive|with '''for'''}} To give (something) in [[exchange]] (for).
#: {{syn|en|exchange|swap|switch|truck|id4=trade}}
#: {{ux|en|Will you '''trade''' your precious watch for my earring?}}
# {{lb|en|transitive}} To [[mutually]] [[exchange]] (something) (with).
#: {{ux|en|The rival schoolboys '''traded''' insults and punches.}}
# {{lb|en|transitive|with '''on'''}} To use or exploit a particular aspect, such as a name, reputation, or image, to gain advantage or benefit.
#: {{syn|en|exploit|[[capitalize]] on|[[take advantage]] of|use|leverage|[[benefit]] from|[[make use]] of|milk}}
#: {{ux|en|Some musicians try to '''trade on''' their past success by playing the same hits over and over again.}}
# {{lb|en|gardening|transitive|or|intransitive}} To [[give]] someone a [[plant]] and [[receive]] a [[different]] one in [[return]].
# {{lb|en|ambitransitive}} To do business; offer for sale as for one's [[livelihood]].
#: {{syn|en|do business}}
# {{lb|en|intransitive}} To have dealings; to be concerned or associated (with).
#* {{RQ:Shakespeare Macbeth|III|v|passage=Saucy and over bold, how did you dare / To '''trade''' and traffic with Macbeth}}
# {{lb|en|transitive}} To [[recommend]] and get [[recommendation]]s.
#: {{syn|en|exchange}}

==English==

===Etymology===
{{root|en|ine-pro|*deh₃-}}
From {{inh|en|enm|adden}}, from {{der|en|la|addō||add, give unto}}.

===Pronunciation===
* {{IPA|en|/æd/}}, {{enPR|ăd}}
* {{audio|en|en-us-add.ogg|a=US}}
* {{rhymes|en|æd|s=1}}
* {{homophones|en|ad}}

===Verb===
{{en-verb}}

# {{lb|en|transitive}} To [[join]] or [[unite]] (e.g. one thing to another, or as several [[particular]]s) so as to increase the number, augment the quantity{{,}} or enlarge the magnitude, or so as to form into one aggregate.
# To [[sum up]]; to put together mentally; to [[add up]].
#: {{co|en|to '''add''' numbers}}
#* {{RQ:Locke Human Understanding|text={{...}}as easily as he can '''add''' together the ideas of two days or two years.}}
#* {{RQ:Guardian|author=Alec Wilkinson|title=Could learning algebra in my 60s make me smarter?|url=https://www.theguardian.com/books/2022/aug/07/could-learning-algebra-in-my-60s-make-me-smarter-alec-wilkinson-a-divine-language-extract|date=2022-08-07|passage=I could '''add''' and subtract and multiply and divide, but I entered the wilderness when words became equations.|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20230322221914/https://www.theguardian.com/books/2022/aug/07/could-learning-algebra-in-my-60s-make-me-smarter-alec-wilkinson-a-divine-language-extract}}
# {{lb|en|transitive}} To combine elements of (something) into one quantity.
#: {{co|en|to '''add''' a column of numbers}}
# {{lb|en|transitive}} To give by way of increased possession (to someone); to bestow (on).
#* {{RQ:KJV|Genesis|30|24|passage=The {{smallcaps|Lord}} shall '''add''' to me another son.}}
#* {{RQ:Milton Paradise Lost|passage=Back to thy punishment, False fugitive, and to thy speed '''add''' wings.|year=1873}}
# {{lb|en|transitive}} To append (e.g. a statement); to say further information.
#* {{RQ:Macaulay History of England|volume=3|page=37|text=He '''added''' that he would willingly consent to the entire abolition of the tax}}
#* {{RQ:Baum Wizard of Oz|chapter=23|passage="Bless your dear heart," she said, "I am sure I can tell you of a way to get back to Kansas." Then she '''added''', "But, if I do, you must give me the Golden Cap."}}
# {{lb|en|intransitive}} To intensify; to augment; to increase.
#: {{ux|en|It '''adds''' to our anxiety.}}
#* {{RQ:KJV|1 Kings|12|14|passage=I will '''add''' to your yoke}}
#* {{RQ:Economist|date=2013-06-29|volume=407|issue=8842|page=72–3
|title=[http://www.economist.com/news/international/science-and-technology/21580133-how-microbes-promote-liver-cancer-overweight-punch-gut A punch in the gut]
|passage=Mostly, the microbiome is beneficial.{{...}}Research over the past few years, however, has implicated it in diseases from atherosclerosis to asthma to autism. Dr Yoshimoto and his colleagues would like to '''add''' liver cancer to that list.}}
# {{lb|en|intransitive|mathematics}} To perform the arithmetical operation of [[addition]].
#: {{ux|en|He '''adds''' rapidly.}}
# {{lb|en|intransitive|video games}} To summon [[minion]]s or [[reinforcement]]s.
#: {{ux|en|Typically, a hostile mob will '''add''' whenever it's within the aggro radius of a player.}}
# {{lb|en|transitive|Internet|text messaging|video games}} To add someone as a friend.

====Usage notes====
* To ''add'' quantities; to ''join'' houses; to ''annex'' territory; to ''unite'' kingdoms; to make parties ''coalesce''.

=====Usage notes=====
* The singular form {{m|en||ship}} is sometimes used without any [[Appendix:Glossary#article|article]], producing such sentences as "In all, we spent three weeks aboard ship." and "Abandon ship!". (Similar patterns may be seen with many place nouns, such as {{m|en|camp}}, {{m|en|home}}, {{m|en|work}}, and {{m|en|school}}, but the details vary between them.)
* Ships were traditionally regarded as ladies, especially by the sailor, and the pronouns {{m|en|her}} and {{m|en|she}} are still sometimes used instead of {{m|en|it}}, though this usage is in decline.

to be necessary. #* {{RQ:Locke Human Understanding|21|143|edition=2nd|text=When we have done it, we have done our duty, and all that is in our power, and indeed all that '''needs'''.}} #* {{quote-journal|en|date=2013-06-28|author=w:Joris Luyendijk| volume=189| issue=3| page=21| magazine=w:The Guardian Weekly| title=[http://www.guardian.co.uk/commentisfree/joris-luyendijk-banking-blog/2013/jun/19/banking-britain-beyond-control Our banks are out of control]| passage=Seeing the British establishment struggle with the financial sector is like watching an alcoholic who still resists the idea that something drastic '''needs''' to happen for him to turn his life around.}} # {{lb|en|obsolete|transitive}} To be [[necessary]] (to someone). #* {{RQ:Spenser Faerie Queene|book=II|canto=IX|passage=More ample spirit, then hitherto was wount, / Here '''needes''' me {{...}}}} =====Usage notes===== * The verb {{m|en||need}} is construed in a few different ways: ** With a direct object, as in “I need your help.” ** With a ''to''-infinitive, as in “I need to go.” Here, the subject of {{m|en||need}} serves implicitly as the subject of the infinitive. ** With a clause of the form “for [object] to [verb phrase]”, or simply “[object] to [verb phrase]” as in “I need for this to happen” or “I need this to happen.” In both variants, the object serves as the subject of the infinitive. ** As a modal verb, with a bare infinitive; in negative polarity contexts, such as questions (“Need I say more?” “Need you have paid so much?”), with negative expressions such as {{m|en|not}} (“It need not happen today”; “No one need ever know”), and with similar constructions (“There need only be one”; “it need be signed only by the president”; “I need hardly explain it”). {{m|en||Need}} in this use does not have inflected forms, apart from the contraction {{m|en|needn't|needn’t}}. ** With a gerund-participle, as in “The car needs washing”, or, in some North American dialects, with a past participle, as in “The car needs washed”"[https://ygdp.yale.edu/phenomena/needs-washed Needs washed]" by Zach Maher and Jim Wood, ''Yale Grammatical Diversity Project: English in North America'', 2011 (both meaning roughly “The car needs to be washed”). ** With a direct object and a predicative complement, as in “We need everyone here on time” (meaning roughly “We need everyone to be here on time”) or “I need it gone” (meaning roughly “I need it to be gone”). ** In certain dialects, and colloquially in certain others, with an unmarked reflexive pronoun, as in “I need me a car.” * A sentence such as “I need you to sit down” or “you need to sit down” is more polite than the bare command “sit down”, but less polite than “please sit down”. It is considered somewhat condescending and infantilizing, hence dubbed by some “the kindergarten imperative”, but is quite common in American usage.“[http://www.slate.com/id/2145734 You Need To Read This: How need to vanquished have to, must, and should.]” by Ben Yagoda, Slate, July 17, 2006 =====Conjugation===== {{en-conj|old=1}} =====Synonyms===== * {{sense|desire}} {{l|en|desire}},
